title: Truly subquadratic algorithms for 3SUM
formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.
why: 3SUM is a central test of whether apparently quadratic search over pairs can admit a fixed polynomial improvement. Its conjectured hardness supports fine-grained lower bounds for many geometric, graph and data-structure problems. The exact model matters: removing a logarithmic factor, changing integer size or omitting preprocessing costs can make a result look stronger than the improvement asked for here.
status_note: The source problem list and Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat’s modern expected-time formulation were checked on 2026-09-14, together with 2026 preprocessed-3SUM work. A bounded later search found no from-scratch Las Vegas algorithm or general lower bound resolving the explicitly selected polynomial-universe variant.

progress.text: Subquadratic integer algorithms with logarithmic-factor savings are among the results reviewed by the source; they leave a fixed polynomial saving open.
Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat develop reductions from the modern expected-time 3SUM conjecture to set-intersection, graph and data-structure tasks.
ICALP work obtains improved subquadratic-space tradeoffs for preprocessed 3SUM; the model retains a preprocessing phase and does not establish a truly subquadratic from-scratch algorithm.

sentences: 3SUM asks whether a value in one integer list is the sum of values from two other lists.
The target is a fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic running time on a precisely specified word RAM.
The selected variant allows every fixed polynomial integer universe and requires a common exponent saving.
Randomization may change the running time but must never produce an incorrect answer.
Known logarithmic savings and faster queries after preprocessing do not meet the from-scratch target.

definitions:
The size parameter \(n\ge2\) bounds the length of each of the three lists. Repeated values are allowed and do not affect the answer; each chosen value comes from its prescribed list. A triple may contain equal numerical values from different lists. There is no single-list distinctness condition. Integers are supplied explicitly in signed binary and fit in one word of
\[w=\left\lceil(B+3)\log_2(n+1)\right\rceil\]
bits. The target equation is equality of ordinary integers, not congruence modulo the word size.

For each fixed \(B\), a uniform word-RAM algorithm has a finite program independent of \(n\) and of all list contents. Its memory cells contain \(w\)-bit words and are addressed by words. Initially only the input and its lengths are present; other cells are zero. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing a word, copying, comparing, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by a word-specified amount; a shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Division by zero can be defined to return zero. The program may obtain an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word at unit cost. There is no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, real-number operation, oracle or nonuniform lookup table. Any table construction, sorting and preprocessing count toward the runtime. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented by these instructions.

Las Vegas means that the program halts with probability one and every output produced is correct; randomization affects its runtime, not its answer. The required bound means that for each \(B\) there are \(K_B,n_B\) such that the expected number of instructions is at most \(K_B n^{2-\varepsilon}\) on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_B\). Expectation is over the program's random words, followed by a worst case over the input lists. All smaller valid instances must also be decided correctly with finite expected time. No average-case input distribution or reusable preprocessing is supplied.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence claim, including one positive exponent saving uniform over every fixed \(B\), correctness, almost-sure termination and the expected instruction bound; or prove its negation. Negation means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed polynomial universe admits no algorithm meeting that saving. An improvement by logarithmic factors alone, a fast data-structure query after expensive preprocessing, a restricted comparison-tree lower bound, or a Monte Carlo algorithm without the stipulated zero-error guarantee does not settle this selected target.

context_blocks.text: Known algorithms beat \(n^2\) by logarithmic factors. Such bounds are \(o(n^2)\), but they do not give \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). The modern conjecture concerns this latter, truly subquadratic improvement.

The three-set input convention follows the source. The integer word-RAM and polynomial-universe choices distinguish this target from real-RAM variants and from decision trees that charge only selected comparisons. The lower-bound claim is not restricted to a comparison-only instruction set.

Kopelowitz, Pettie and Porat formulate the modern conjecture even for expected running time and use Las Vegas complexities in their reductions. The zero-error convention here follows that formulation; it is made explicit rather than silently identifying different randomized models.

Recent work improves time–space tradeoffs after sets have been preprocessed. This is useful progress for data structures, but the present input arrives from scratch, so the entire preprocessing time must be included in its complexity.
